A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the Primus research work. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, equations, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial additions and reformatting in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original Transformer-removal experiments, Primus development ablations, cross-validation segmentation results, and representational-similarity analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds PrimusV2 experiments, further baseline comparisons, tokenizer ablations, and computational measurements.

M1.justification: v2 introduces PrimusV2 alongside Primus. Its iterative tokenizer replaces the single patch projection with convolutional residual downsampling, creating overlapping, more expressive tokens before the Transformer. This changes a central architectural component rather than merely documenting the original model more fully (Sections 3.2–3.4).

E1.justification: The same nine development/test datasets and the AMOS-CT, KiTS19, and TotalSegmentator-BTCV diagnostic coverage are retained. Appendix F measures random-crop runtime and extrapolates to illustrative clinical volumes; it does not evaluate additional clinical datasets or segmentation tasks.

E2.justification: The main benchmark expands from six comparison methods in v1 Table 6 to eleven in v2 Table 7. MedNeXt-L, UNETR++, SwinUNETR-v2, SegMamba, and VisionxLSTM are newly evaluated, substantially strengthening comparison across CNN, Transformer, state-space, and recurrent architectures.

E3.justification: The core cross-validation splits, preprocessing plans, and training budgets remain unchanged. v2 adds controlled tokenizer comparisons, memory measurements at 50% and 80% masking, and encoder timing using 160-cubed crops with batch size one, excluding preprocessing. The main benchmark now restricts L configurations to development datasets.

E4.justification: New tokenizer ablations compare four alternatives with and without Transformers, testing the tradeoff between accuracy and Transformer dependence (Table 6). v2 also extends dataset-size analysis to Primus-L, adds qualitative segmentation examples, and investigates memory and inference-time feasibility. The earlier Appendix C and E analyses largely remain.

E5.justification: Appendix F newly reports runtime estimation using the median of 100 forward passes. Existing three-seed introspection and CKA comparison procedures are retained; no increase in training repetitions or new segmentation confidence intervals is reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive PrimusV2 and baseline results: Table 7 reports average DSC of 81.43 for PrimusV2-M, 81.48 for ResEnc-L, and 81.72 for MedNeXt-L. Original Primus scores are also revised, and its L-model test-set averages are omitted while fold-0 appendix results remain. Table 13 replaces the unfinished KiTS23 Primus-L/4 entry with 84.79. Memory and runtime results are newly reported.

T1.justification: Appendix F adds a simple analytical runtime model based on the number of 160-cubed crops, prediction time per crop, and a deadline-based applicability criterion. The UNet-index definition and Appendix E's CKA/HSIC equations remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on the first competitive pure Transformer architecture. v2 reframes the contribution as two Transformer-centric families, makes iterative tokenization a principal contribution, and explicitly claims PrimusV2 reaches parity with stronger CNNs including ResEnc-L and MedNeXt.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly defends beneficial CNN–Transformer combinations, explains the stronger tokenizer's role, and acknowledges increased convolutional dependence and token-overlap risks for masked pretraining. It also qualifies retained ablations with a RoPE-error disclosure and adds clinical-applicability arguments from timing. Section 2.2 becomes more categorical about stable performance gaps excluding data scarcity as the limitation.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the new tokenizer's kernels, strides, channels, and residual-block arrangements, plus timing hardware and crop settings. Tables 12–14 newly disclose a legacy 3D RoPE permutation error. The code pointer changes from an author-hosted Primus branch to the nnU-Net project's Primus documentation; existing training hyperparameters and preprocessing tables are largely retained.

R1.justification: Appendix B's historical review is largely retained. v2 extends positioning to state-space and xLSTM competitors and adds references including UNETR++, DINOv3, V-JEPA, Chameleon, and clinical-timing work. Purity-based novelty is qualified as Transformer-centric design, while the central research motivation remains.

P1.justification: Substantial portions of the introduction, diagnostic discussion, method description, and conclusions are rewritten. Method subsections are consolidated, the narrative is reorganized around Primus and PrimusV2, and Appendices F and G are added. These changes exceed routine wording edits.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a single-column journal layout, transposes and expands Table 1, redraws the architecture diagram, expands the benchmark table, and adds tokenizer and timing tables plus qualitative Figure 4. Figure 2 gains a Primus-L panel. The smaller-token results remain in Appendix C despite removal of their separate main-text summary table.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central empirical argument through tokenizer-removal controls and comparisons against stronger, newer baselines (Tables 6–7). These provide evidence addressing v1's small-lesion weakness and performance gap to strong CNNs while demonstrating a measurable Transformer contribution. Explicit convolutional tradeoffs and error disclosures improve transparency. Retained RoPE-error-affected ablations and clinical claims based only on encoder timing remain limitations, but do not outweigh the stronger experimental support and more precise architectural positioning.
